prompt: Write an essay titled “Detonating A Huge Pile of Lead Azide. Really.”. It is a chemist's question-and-answer commentary on the US Army's plan to detonate a large quantity of the primary explosive lead azide near Burlington, Iowa. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
I recently came across a news item stating that the US Army plans to dispose of a large stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, just outside Burlington, by piling it up and detonating it in the open air. As a chemist, my immediate reaction was a mixture of professional fascination and profound, visceral dread. Since a few people have asked me why this sounds like such a terrible idea, let’s walk through the chemistry of what is actually happening here.

**First of all, what exactly is lead azide?**

Lead azide, $\text{Pb(N}_3)_2$, is what we call a primary explosive. Most people are familiar with secondary explosives like TNT, RDX, or C-4. Those materials are remarkably stable; you can drop them, hit them with a hammer, or even set them on fire, and they usually won't detonate. They require a sharp, violent shockwave to get going. Primary explosives are what provide that shockwave. They are the hair-trigger materials used inside blasting caps and detonators. 

Lead azide is famously, aggressively sensitive to friction, static electricity, and impact. Chemically, it consists of a lead atom attached to two azide groups—chains of three nitrogen atoms. Nitrogen atoms are never happier than when they are paired up as triple-bonded $\text{N}_2$ gas, and they will release a tremendous amount of energy to get there. A single crystal of dry lead azide cracking under its own weight, or scraping against the side of a metal container, can be enough to set off the entire batch.

**So why on earth is there a "huge pile" of it in Iowa?**

Because the military has been manufacturing, storing, and dismantling munitions for decades, and primary explosives do not age gracefully. You normally only use a few milligrams of lead azide in a single detonator. Accumulating hundreds or thousands of pounds of the stuff—whether from off-spec manufacturing batches or demilitarized Cold War ordnance—is an inevitable byproduct of industrial warfare. It is also a massive liability. You do not want tons of a hyper-sensitive primary explosive sitting in a bunker indefinitely, waiting for a stray spark, a temperature swing, or a clumsy forklift driver.

**If it’s that sensitive, how do they even move it to a detonation site without blowing themselves up?**

Very, very carefully, and almost certainly wet. Lead azide is typically stored and transported submerged in water or a water-alcohol mixture, often formulated with a desensitizing agent like dextrin to keep the crystals from growing too large and brittle. Wet lead azide is significantly less touchy than the dry powder, though "less touchy" is a relative term that still makes most synthetic chemists break out in a cold sweat. Even with those precautions, the logistics of scooping, hauling, and staging large quantities of a primary explosive for open-air detonation is a terrifying bit of materials handling.

**Okay, so it's dangerous to move. Once it's in the pit and they blow it up, the problem is solved, right?**

Not if you believe in the conservation of mass. Let’s look at the reaction: $\text{Pb(N}_3)_2$ decomposes into nitrogen gas and elemental lead. The nitrogen is completely harmless; it makes up nearly eighty percent of the air we breathe. The lead, however, does not magically vanish when you detonate it. You cannot destroy an element with a chemical explosion. 

Instead, the extreme heat and pressure of the blast vaporize the heavy metal and launch it into the atmosphere, where it cools into a finely divided, toxic aerosol of lead and lead oxide dust. Open-air detonation is essentially an extraordinarily efficient mechanism for turning a contained pile of toxic metal into a breathable, bioavailable cloud, right next to the Mississippi River and the town of Burlington.

**Surely there is a better, non-explosive way to get rid of it?**

In a laboratory, yes. Chemists routinely destroy small amounts of azides by reacting them with nitrous acid—usually generated by mixing sodium nitrite with a dilute acid—which converts the azide into harmless nitrogen gas and nitrous oxide. You can also use ceric ammonium nitrate. Scaling that up to handle thousands of pounds of a shock-sensitive solid, however, is its own special nightmare. If you add the acid too quickly or lose temperature control, you generate hydrazoic acid ($\text{HN}_3$), which is both wildly toxic and violently explosive as a vapor. Even if everything goes smoothly, you are left with massive vats of acidic, lead-contaminated liquid waste that still requires expensive remediation.

**So the Army is choosing the explosion because it's easier?**

Essentially, yes. Open burning and open detonation—OB/OD, in military parlance—is the traditional, cheap, and fast way to make energetic waste disappear from the inventory sheet. When you are staring down a bunker full of aging primary explosives, the urge to just rig a remote detonator, retreat to a safe distance, and push the button is deeply understandable. It is just unfortunate that in this case, pushing the button means dusting the local zip code with aerosolized lead. As a chemist, I appreciate the desire to get rid of lead azide as quickly as possible. I just wouldn't want to be standing downwind when they do it.
